clinicalPearls: Caused by pathogenic variants in IQSEC2 on Xp11.22, encoding a brain-enriched guanine nucleotide exchange factor for the small GTPase ARF6 at excitatory postsynaptic densities.

Unusual for an X-linked gene: de novo variants cause severe encephalopathy in both sexes, and heterozygous girls are frequently affected as severely as hemizygous boys because the gene partially escapes X-inactivation and is dosage sensitive.
Phenotype spans a spectrum from milder non-syndromic intellectual disability (often inherited hypomorphic missense variants in males) to severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy.
Rett-like features — hand stereotypies, developmental regression and acquired microcephaly — occur, especially in girls; consider IQSEC2 when MECP2, CDKL5 and FOXG1 testing is negative.
Epilepsy is common and frequently drug-resistant, with infantile spasms and multiple seizure types; the EEG may evolve towards a Lennox-Gastaut-like pattern.
Truncating variants tend to produce the most severe phenotypes, while pathogenic missense variants cluster in the IQ-like, catalytic Sec7 and PH domains.
Autism, stereotypies, self-injurious or aggressive behaviour, hypotonia, gait disturbance and disrupted sleep are frequent accompaniments.
Diagnosis rests on molecular testing (exome or an epilepsy/intellectual disability gene panel); management is supportive and symptomatic with no disease-specific therapy.
reference.pathophysiology: IQSEC2 (Xp11.22) encodes IQ motif and Sec7 domain-containing protein 2, a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) for the small GTPase ARF6 (ADP-ribosylation factor 6). The protein is concentrated in the postsynaptic density of excitatory glutamatergic synapses, where it binds the scaffolding protein PSD-95 and, through cyclical activation of ARF6, governs actin cytoskeletal remodelling, dendritic spine morphology and the trafficking and internalisation of AMPA-type glutamate receptors — processes central to synaptic strength and plasticity. Loss-of-function (truncating) variants and missense variants within the IQ-like, catalytic Sec7 or pleckstrin homology domains disrupt this GEF activity and downstream synaptic signalling. Because IQSEC2 partially escapes X-inactivation and is dosage sensitive, heterozygous females carrying de novo variants can be as severely affected as hemizygous males, whereas some inherited hypomorphic missense alleles in males produce a milder, non-syndromic intellectual disability.
additionalDifferentials: Other X-linked intellectual disability disorders (e.g. ARX-related, Christianson syndrome/SLC9A6)
Other genetic developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (STXBP1, SCN2A, SYNGAP1)
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing — exome sequencing or a targeted epilepsy/intellectual disability gene panel including IQSEC2
Interictal and prolonged/video EEG for seizure and epilepsy-syndrome characterisation
Brain MRI (frequently normal or non-specific; helps exclude structural and alternative causes)
Structured developmental, neuropsychological and autism assessment
Parental segregation testing to establish de novo versus inherited status
X-inactivation studies in affected females as an interpretive adjunct
Targeted metabolic screen where clinically indicated to exclude mimics
redFlags: New, worsening or prolonged drug-resistant seizures, including status epilepticus, requiring urgent review
Developmental regression or loss of previously acquired skills
Self-injurious behaviour or feeding and swallowing difficulty with aspiration risk
reference.prognosis: Outcome is variable but often guarded: severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy is associated with profound intellectual disability, absent speech and drug-resistant epilepsy, whereas inherited hypomorphic missense variants in males may cause milder, non-progressive intellectual disability. Long-term outlook is largely determined by seizure severity and associated complications.
pitfalls: Assuming an X-linked gene spares females — girls with de novo IQSEC2 variants are frequently severely affected and may be mislabelled as Rett syndrome.
Overlooking IQSEC2 once first-line Rett/encephalopathy genes (MECP2, CDKL5, FOXG1) return negative.
Reporting missense variants of uncertain significance without domain and segregation context.
Attributing regression solely to seizures and missing the underlying genetic diagnosis.
Failing to identify and counsel carrier females in families with apparently non-syndromic X-linked intellectual disability.
references: Clinical genetics and neurogenetics reference texts
Paediatric epilepsy and developmental and epileptic encephalopathy consensus reviews
management: Treat epilepsy with antiseizure medication, using hormonal therapy (corticotropin or corticosteroids) or vigabatrin for infantile spasms
Manage frequently drug-resistant seizures with rational combination therapy and consider the ketogenic diet
Provide developmental support through early intervention, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and augmentative communication support
Address Rett-like features, hand stereotypies and behavioural or autistic symptoms with tailored behavioural and supportive measures
Confirm the diagnosis by molecular genetic testing and characterise seizures with prolonged or video EEG
Offer genetic counselling with parental segregation testing to establish de novo versus inherited status and inform family planning
Coordinate multidisciplinary care under paediatric neurology with allied health and family support
